captive_summary: Cancelled-and-never-built: Korea Southern Power (KOSPO) withdrew the Hadong LNG Storage Facility project at an April 22, 2024 board meeting. The completed basic design scope was storage tanks + vaporization/send-out facilities + a berthing dock only — no generation was ever part of the design. The terminal's business case depended on supplying a separate, adjacent 4-unit LNG power project; Korea's 11th Basic Power Supply and Demand Plan reassigned those units elsewhere (unit 4 to Goyang/Changnyeong, units 5-6 to Yongin), cutting the associated LNG power capacity from 2GW to 1GW and killing the terminal's rationale.
confirmed_how: OhMyNews (2024-04-22) and Energy Platform News both report the KOSPO board's withdrawal decision and quote the same environmental-group framing ("경영환경변화로 LNG터미널의 사업성 확보가 불가능해지자"). Energy Platform News additionally quotes the design scope verbatim: "저장탱크, 기화시설, 접안부두" (storage tanks, vaporization facilities, berthing facilities) at the Hadong coal power plant site, and explains the redirected LNG power units as the reason the terminal became unviable.

notes: Direction-test case even hypothetically: had it been built, the terminal's whole purpose was to supply fuel to a separate LNG power project on an adjacent site, not to self-power — never a captive candidate.

captive_summary: Under-construction commercial LNG storage/regas/trading hub (Myodo Island, Yeosu; JV of BS Hanyang 60% / GS Energy 40%; phase 1 targeted 2027). The developer's own official facilities page gives a complete equipment inventory — four 200,000 m³ storage tanks, a 100,000 DWT berth, ORV (seawater) 140 t/h × 4 plus SCV (combustion) 140 t/h × 2 vaporizers, and 5.2 km of high-pressure pipeline to the Yeosu industrial complex — with no generation component, and separately touts 'cold-energy utilization' (냉열 에너지 활용) supplied to the industrial park, which is a non-combustion byproduct use, not captive gas power. The terminal's stated purpose is distributing LNG for industrial and power-generation use in the Yeosu/Gwangyang complexes — fuel flows OUT, not power IN.
confirmed_how: Official project site (nea-lng.com) facilities page lists every major system (storage, dock, ORV/SCV vaporization, pipeline network, cold-energy use) with no generation equipment mentioned; this is a primary developer disclosure describing the full as-designed/as-built scope, consistent with multiple press descriptions (Yonhap, Financial Today, Kukmin Ilbo) of the terminal as a distribution/trading hub feeding the Yeosu/Gwangyang industrial complexes.

captive_summary: KOGAS's original 1986 flagship LNG base, handling ~40% of national gas supply and feeding the national pipeline network plus several colocated/nearby merchant power plants (Pyeongtaek Thermal, Gumi CCGT already in GEM's PowerPlantsSupplied field; also identified in this research: Shin Pyeongtaek power station, a separate 950 MW gas IPP owned by a GS Energy / Korea Western Power / KB Asset Management joint venture, commissioned 2019, unrelated to KOGAS). No public source was found, despite extensive search, that states whether the KOGAS base itself has on-site backup/captive gas generation or is purely grid-fed. captive_summary: KOGAS's third LNG base (construction from 1997; three 140,000 m³ tanks; ~21.3% of national LNG supply). The colocated GOGPT-prior plant, Tongyeong Eco Power, is confirmed via HDC Holdings' own site as a separate merchant power company (HDC Group, in partnership with Hanwha Energy; 1,012 MW LNG combined-cycle; commercial operation Oct 29 2024) that is 'directly connected to KOGAS Tongyeong base LNG supply equipment' but procures its own LNG fuel via its own 210,000 kℓ storage facility — a supply relationship (direction: terminal → plant), not captive power into the terminal. That settles the GOGPT-prior question. It does NOT, however, establish whether the KOGAS base itself has separate on-site backup/captive generation — no source found either way for that narrower question.

captive_summary: Ulsan LNG Terminal is operated by Korea Energy Terminal Co. (KET), a joint venture of Korea National Oil Corp (52.4%) and SK Gas (47.6%), whose entire described business is unloading, storage, regasification, and send-out (three tanks, 645,000 kℓ combined). KET supplies 900,000-1,000,000 t/yr of regasified LNG to Ulsan GPS, a separate 1.2 GW LNG/LPG combined-cycle power station (SK Gas subsidiary) located ~5-20 minutes away by road — the terminal's own PowerPlantsSupplied field already documents this relationship. This is the direction-test pattern explicitly: fuel flows OUT of the terminal to the power plant, not captive power IN.
confirmed_how: E2News feature article and iNews24 report both independently confirm KET and Ulsan GPS are separate companies/facilities, with KET supplying 900,000-1,000,000 t/yr of LNG to Ulsan GPS (1.2 GW, SK Gas subsidiary, ~5 km/20 min away); iNews24 additionally gives KET's ownership split (KNOC 52.4% / SK Gas 47.6%) and tank specs.
